## Strip the short notes and a skeleton falls out

Take a melody, delete everything between its long arrivals, and you're usually
left with a plain harmonic outline. Put the short notes back and the line gets
its momentum, its delays and its small detours again. Some of the notes you
restored don't belong to the harmony sounding underneath them. They still make
sense, because of how they arrive and where they go next.

Four names for four behaviours. A *passing tone* fills the step between two
chord tones. A *neighbour tone* steps away from a chord tone and comes straight
back. A *suspension* holds a note from the previous harmony into the next one
before resolving down. An *anticipation* arrives at a note of the coming chord
before the chord does.

Every one of those describes behaviour across time. Show me a pitch on its own
and I can't tell you which role it's playing. That's the whole lesson.

## Four versions of the same outline

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 88
use_synth :piano

define :play_phrase do |events|
  events.each do |pitch, duration|
    play pitch, release: duration * 0.82
    sleep duration
  end
end

skeleton = [[:c4, 2], [:e4, 2], [:g4, 2], [:c5, 2]]

passing = [[:c4, 1], [:d4, 1], [:e4, 2],
           [:g4, 1], [:a4, 1], [:c5, 2]]

neighbor = [[:c4, 1], [:d4, 0.5], [:c4, 0.5], [:e4, 2],
            [:g4, 1], [:f4, 0.5], [:g4, 0.5], [:c5, 2]]

decorated = [[:c4, 1], [:d4, 1], [:e4, 1], [:f4, 1],
             [:g4, 1], [:a4, 0.5], [:b4, 0.5], [:c5, 2]]

[skeleton, passing, neighbor, decorated].each do |events|
  play_phrase events
  sleep 1
end
```

The skeleton gives you four long targets and almost no motion between them. In
`passing`, D fills the step from C to E, and the later A puts motion between G
and C without walking every rung of the ladder. The neighbours circle away from
a target and return. The last version thickens as it approaches the final C,
which hands the same harmonic outline a sense of direction.

Play the skeleton and the decorated version back to back. Are those the same
melody? There's a real argument either way, and it's the argument this lesson
is about.

## Three edits, and one of them needs new scaffolding

1. Change D in the passing line to D-sharp. It still sits between C and E, but
   now the two steps are unequal, and the chromatic approach puts a harder
   emphasis on E.

2. There's no harmony timeline in that program, so you'll have to add one before
   you can test a suspension. Hold F major for two beats, move to C major for
   two, sustain F across the boundary, then resolve it down to E. F starts life
   as a chord tone and turns dissonant only when the harmony moves underneath it.

3. Use the same timeline for an anticipation. Move the final C half a beat
   earlier than the C major chord. The note becomes stable when the harmony
   catches up with it. Without that chord boundary in the data, the label has
   nothing to stand on.

## Why the label needs a clock

Chord membership is a question about a moment. C is stable over C major, it
decorates plenty of other harmonies, and it can anticipate an A minor chord
that hasn't arrived. To classify a melodic event, your program needs the
harmony lined up against that event's onset and duration. The note value alone
gets you nowhere.

Reduction picks the notes that look structurally stable, usually from metric
position, duration and harmonic membership. Decoration then explains the routes
between them. It's interpretive, and it throws information away. When rhythm or
harmony is ambiguous, two defensible reductions keep different skeletons, and
playing both turns an analytical disagreement into something you can hear.

The arrays here keep pitch next to duration. A richer event could carry a
`:role` field, and playback would still consume only the note and the timing.
Role belongs to the analysis, not to the act of rendering a pitch. Keep those
apart and you can change your interpretation without quietly rewriting the
melody underneath it.

Metric position moves the reading more than you'd expect. A dissonant step on a
weak half-beat slips by. Sustain that same pitch across a strong beat and it
demands a bigger explanation, probably as a suspension. Duration, preparation
and destination all weigh in. Set membership will flag a non-chord tone for you.
It can't name the behaviour without looking at the neighbours in time.

Reduction works as a composing method too. Start from stable destinations, then
decide whether each gap wants direct motion, a delay, or a quick departure and
return. Add one decoration and replay. Decorate every opening and the
destinations lose their hierarchy, which is a real cost and easy to miss. The
alternating versions above keep that trade-off in front of your ears.

## Label your own decorations

Write a two-bar melody over C major followed by G major. Include one passing
tone, one neighbour, one suspension and one anticipation, and label each role in
an event hash holding `:note`, `:start`, `:duration` and `:role`. Your renderer
must ignore the analytical field entirely.

Then print and play a reduction containing only the `:chord_tone` events, and
compare those bare destinations against the full line. Check that every
decoration can be explained by where it came from and where it went. If one
can't, either it's in the wrong place or your label is wrong, and deciding which
is exactly the skill this lesson is for.
